title: Cutaneous Leishmaniasis
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a sand‑fly transmitted protozoal infection causing chronic skin ulcers. Diagnosis relies on lesion microscopy or PCR; treatment is systemic or local antimonials, with alternatives for resource‑limited settings.

sections.p: Leishmaniasis is caused by intracellular Leishmania parasites transmitted by female Phlebotomus (Old World) or Lutzomyia (New World) sand flies. In East Africa, L. aethiopica and L. tropica predominate, producing skin‑limited disease that may persist for months.
b: Lesions start as papules, evolve to nodules, then ulcerate with raised borders
Usually single lesion, but multiple lesions occur in immunocompromised hosts

sections.p: Leishmania are obligate intracellular flagellates that survive within macrophage phagolysosomes as amastigotes. Species differ in geographic distribution and propensity for mucocutaneous spread.
b: Promastigotes: flagellated form in sand‑fly gut

sections.p: Infected sand‑fly bites deposit promastigotes into the dermis. Parasites are phagocytosed, transform to amastigotes, replicate, and infect new macrophages. Human‑to‑human transmission is rare, occurring only via contaminated needles or organ transplantation.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis presents with chronic ulcerative skin lesions. Severity is staged by size, number, location, and host immunity. Complications include secondary bacterial infection, scarring, and, in L. aethiopica, mucosal involvement.
b: Mild: ≤2 cm ulcer, single lesion, no mucosal spread
Severe: >5 cm, >3 lesions, or mucosal extension

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, bedside microscopy of a slit‑skin smear is the mainstay. When unavailable, clinical criteria and epidemiology guide treatment; referral for PCR or culture is ideal when possible.

t.b: Confirms Leishmania amastigotes; positive result = definitive diagnosis
Shows intracellular amastigotes; used when smear is negative
Species identification; guides therapy if available
Serology; supportive but less specific for cutaneous disease

sections.p: First‑line therapy in East Africa is systemic sodium stibogluconate (SSG) for lesions >2 cm or mucosal risk. Local options (cryotherapy, intralesional SSG, thermotherapy) are preferred for small, uncomplicated lesions. Preventive measures focus on vector control and personal protection.
b: Systemic SSG: kills intracellular amastigotes; monitor renal and cardiac function
Miltefosine (oral): alternative where SSG unavailable; avoid in pregnancy
Cryotherapy: liquid nitrogen; effective for ≤2 cm lesions, minimal systemic toxicity
Thermotherapy: 50 °C probe; useful where electricity is reliable

sections.p: Think CL in any patient from an endemic area with a chronic ulcer that began as a papule, especially if a sand‑fly bite is recalled. Remember that immunosuppression (HIV, malnutrition) increases lesion number and risk of mucosal spread.
b: Never rely solely on culture in low‑resource hospitals; smear is adequate
If SSG contraindicated, use miltefosine or local therapy
Watch for secondary bacterial infection—treat with appropriate antibiotics

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid lesion expansion, signs of secondary infection (pus, erythema, fever)
Systemic toxicity from antimonial therapy (renal failure, cardiac arrhythmia)

faq.q: Why is a skin smear preferred over serology?
faq.a: The smear directly visualises the parasite in the lesion, confirming active disease; antibodies may be absent or cross‑reactive.

faq.q: Can cutaneous leishmaniasis heal without treatment?
faq.a: Spontaneous healing can occur over months, but it leaves disfiguring scars and may progress to mucosal disease, so treatment is recommended.

faq.q: What is the role of HIV co‑infection?
faq.a: HIV impairs macrophage function, leading to multiple, larger lesions and higher risk of visceral spread.

exam: A 28‑year‑old farmer from northern Kenya presents with a 3 cm ulcer on the forearm, papular onset 6 weeks ago. What is your next diagnostic step — Perform a slit‑skin smear to look for amastigotes.
In a patient with multiple facial lesions and HIV, which systemic drug is preferred and why — Sodium stibogluconate because it penetrates macrophages and covers possible mucosal spread.

A small 1 cm lesion on the cheek of a child from Ethiopia is diagnosed clinically as CL but SSG is unavailable. What alternative therapy is appropriate — Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, as it is effective for lesions ≤2 cm and avoids systemic toxicity.

During antimonial therapy the patient develops rising creatinine and QT prolongation. What should you do — Stop SSG, switch to miltefosine if pregnancy is excluded, and manage renal/ cardiac complications.
How does vector control reduce CL incidence in low‑resource settings — Use insecticide‑treated bed nets, indoor residual spraying, and environmental management to lower sand‑fly contact.

A patient with a chronic ulcer is misdiagnosed as bacterial cellulitis and given antibiotics only. What key clinical clue would have pointed to CL — History of sand‑fly bite and lesion evolution from papule to ulcer with raised indurated border.
What complication distinguishes L. aethiopica infection from L. tropica — Higher propensity for mucosal involvement and treatment resistance, requiring systemic therapy.
If PCR is unavailable, how can you still stage disease severity — Use lesion size, number, location, and host immune status (e.g., HIV) to apply the mild/moderate/severe classification.
